Almost every face has small differences between sides, and this is entirely normal. A symmetry test shows these differences in a photo, but it does not decide how attractive anyone is. How do I check my face symmetry? Upload a front-facing, level photo, confirm you have permission to use it, and run the test. You can look through the example images on this page and read every answer here without paying anything. Is the face symmetry test accurate? It is a visual guide, not a calibrated measurement. Guide points are illustrative, and we do not give exact numbers. Head tilt, lens distortion, hair and expression all change how symmetrical a face looks in a photo. What photo works best for checking symmetry? Use a straight-on photo with your head level, a neutral or relaxed expression and soft, even light. Hold the camera at eye level and a little farther away. Tilted or wide-angle selfies make faces look less symmetrical. Is a symmetrical face more attractive? Not necessarily. Some research links symmetry with perceived attractiveness, but many admired faces are noticeably asymmetrical, and small differences often add character. Verified Glam ("we," "us," or "our") operates the Verified Glam - Beauty Scanner website and the Verified Glam mobile application for Android (package com.verifiedglam.beauty_scanner). This Privacy Policy explains how we collect, use, disclose, and safeguard your information when you use our app or contact us. 1. Information we collect Photos and scan data. When you run a beauty scan, you upload or capture a selfie. We store your photo (and any second photo for two-photo features) in secure cloud storage and process it to generate analysis results. Account and profile information. If you create an account, we collect identifiers such as your email address and profile details you provide during onboarding. Device and usage data. We may collect standard app analytics such as device type, operating system version, app version, and feature usage to improve stability and performance. Advertising and subscriptions. Free users may see ads served by Google AdMob. If you subscribe to Pro, purchase and subscription status are processed through Polar.sh (hosted checkout). Your account is linked via your user ID for cross-platform access on web and Android. Support communications. If you email us at support@verifiedglam.com, we retain the content of your message and your email address to respond to you. 2. How we use your information Provide AI-powered beauty analysis and display results in the app Store scan history and thumbnails associated with your account Authenticate you and maintain your profile and preferences Deliver ads to free-tier users and manage Pro subscriptions Send push notifications if you opt in Improve the app, fix bugs, and prevent abuse or fraud Comply with legal obligations 3. AI processing Facial analysis is performed on our servers using third-party AI services (including OpenAI). Your photos are sent to these services only for the purpose of generating your requested scan results. API keys and AI credentials are kept on the server — they are never embedded in the mobile app. AI outputs are generated automatically and may not always be accurate. They are intended for entertainment and self-discovery, not medical or professional advice. Celebrity Look-Alike uses TMDB to find a real published photo of your matched celebrity when one is available. When it isn't, we generate a synthetic, AI-created image intended to resemble that celebrity for entertainment purposes only — this is clearly labeled as an AI impression in the app and is never presented as an actual photo of that person. This product uses the TMDB API but is not endorsed or certified by TMDB. 4. How we store and protect data We use Cloudflare (Workers, D1 database, and R2 storage) for authentication, database records, and private storage of scan photos. Access to your data is protected by account authentication and server-side access controls. 5. We may disclose information if required by law or to protect our rights, users, or safety. 6. Children's privacy Verified Glam - Beauty Scanner is not directed at children or teens. We do not knowingly collect personal information from anyone under 18. International users Your information may be processed in countries where our service providers operate. By using the app, you consent to such transfers subject to applicable safeguards. 10. /blog/find-your-face-shape-from-a-photo.body: How to find your face shape from a photo | AI Beauty Styling Why a photo is a fair starting point Face shape is a way of describing the outline of a face: how wide the forehead, cheekbones and jaw are in relation to each other, and how long the face looks overall. Common labels include oval, round, square, heart and diamond. They are shorthand used by stylists and makeup artists so that two people can talk about a silhouette without a ruler. A photograph is a reasonable place to start because it freezes the outline and lets you study it calmly. It also has limits. A camera flattens a three-dimensional head into two dimensions, and the result depends heavily on lens, distance and angle. Treat anything you read from a single picture as a first impression that you can test with a second photo. Start with a useful photo Choose a front-facing portrait taken near eye level. Pull hair away from the sides of your face if you can, and avoid a wide-angle selfie taken very close to the camera. Lens distortion, a strong tilt and deep shadows can change the outline you are trying to see. You do not need a perfectly symmetrical image. You only need a clear view of the forehead, cheekbones and jaw. If the first image is heavily filtered, try a second, unedited photo before drawing a conclusion. Soft daylight from a window in front of you works better than an overhead bulb, which carves shadows under the brows and chin. Compare the broad proportions Look at which part appears widest. A wider forehead with a narrower chin can suggest a heart-like outline; similar width through the forehead, cheeks and jaw can read more square; gentle curves and a longer overall outline often read oval; widest cheekbones with a narrower forehead and jaw point toward diamond. Many faces sit between these descriptions, and that is normal. If you would like help looking, the Face Shape Analyzer places an overview of your outline beside your photo so you can see which description fits best. For a more detailed look at where the main features sit, the Facial Landmarks Map gives an illustrative guide to visible features. Both are visual aids for exploring a photo, not anatomical measurements. The label is a shorthand for discussing a silhouette, not a verdict about your features. Small changes in expression, hairstyle and camera angle can move the apparent outline from one category toward another. If you want to understand why one angle can change how balanced a face looks, read our guide to what a facial symmetry preview can and cannot show . Use the result as a styling reference If you are planning a haircut, bring both your portrait and a few styles you like. A stylist can account for hair density, texture and how much time you want to spend styling it. The shape guide can help you explain what you want to emphasize, but it should not tell you which cuts you are allowed to wear. A visual preview makes this easier. With the Hairstyle Changer you can see a few different cuts on your own portrait and compare the full picture, not just the face outline. Our guide on how to plan a hair change with a photo preview explains what to look at first. Glasses, necklines and earrings are also easier to think about once you know which areas of your outline you would like to balance or echo. As with hair, treat any suggestion as an idea to try rather than a rule. Common mistakes to avoid The most frequent mistake is judging from a selfie taken at arm's length. Close, wide-angle shots enlarge whatever is nearest the lens, usually the nose and forehead, and make the jaw look narrower. Step back, zoom in a little, and hold the phone at eye level. Another mistake is treating a label as a limit. Nobody needs permission to wear a fringe, a short crop or a bold frame because of a category. Labels describe common patterns; real faces are a mixture, and they change with expression, age and lighting. Finally, avoid comparing yourself with edited photos. Filters and beauty modes smooth and reshape the outline, so a portrait that has been through an app can give you a misleading answer. Use an untouched image whenever you can. How the five common shapes are usually described Oval faces are usually described as longer than they are wide, with a forehead slightly wider than the chin and softly curved edges. Round faces have similar length and width, with fuller cheeks and a rounded chin and jawline. Square faces have a broad forehead and a strong, angular jaw, with width that stays fairly even from top to bottom. Heart-shaped faces are widest at the forehead and taper to a narrower chin, often with high cheekbones. Diamond faces are narrowest at the forehead and jaw and widest across the cheekbones. These are descriptions of tendencies, and most people recognize parts of two or three of them in themselves. How hair and frames change the picture Hair has a large effect on how a face outline is perceived. A middle parting with hair tucked behind the ears shows the full forehead and jaw, while a heavy fringe hides the forehead and shortens the face. Volume at the crown adds length, and volume at the sides adds width. This is why many stylists ask to see your hair pulled back before suggesting a cut. Glasses work in a similar way. A frame that is wider than the cheekbones can make a face look narrower, while a very small frame can make the lower face look larger. Trying a few styles on, either in a shop or in a photo, shows you more than any label can. What to do next Take two or three photos in the same light with a neutral expression, run them through a shape tool if you like, and see whether the answers agree. If they do, you have a reasonable working description. If they do not, that is useful information too: it means your outline sits between categories. /blog/what-facial-symmetry-really-shows.body: What a facial symmetry preview can—and cannot—show Every portrait has a camera angle A symmetry preview compares visible landmarks on the two sides of a photo. It can help you notice how the brows, eyes or jaw appear in that particular frame. It cannot measure your face the way a clinical imaging system would. Even a slight head turn changes what the camera sees. Lighting may make one cheek look fuller, while a phone lens may stretch whichever side is closer. That is why a single photograph is a poor source for absolute claims, and why this site describes its guides as illustrative. What the tool actually draws The Facial Symmetry Test lays a small set of visual guides over your portrait: a centerline, markers for the height of the eyes and brows, and a view of how the two halves of the face compare. These are there to give you context, so that a difference you notice by eye has something to be compared against. The guides are not calibrated. A mark that sits a few pixels higher on one side tells you something about that photograph, not about the structure of your face. If a result includes a number, read it as a subjective impression of the image, similar to how a photographer might comment on balance in a frame. Read a guide, not a grade Natural faces are not mirror images. Expression gives one side a different shape from the other, and that is part of what makes a portrait recognizable. A visual line or side-by-side guide is best understood as a way to explore the composition of a photo. People often assume that perfect symmetry is the goal. It is not. Many faces that people find striking have clear differences between the left and right sides, and a face with exactly mirrored halves can look unnatural. Treat the guide as curiosity, not as a target to reach. Related ways to look at proportion If you like exploring a portrait with guides, two other tools take a different view. The Face Golden Ratio tool shows face thirds and eye spacing next to the idea of phi, which is a reference concept rather than a rule of beauty. The Facial Landmarks Map shows where the main features sit so you can see how the pieces fit together. If you have two portraits and want to see how they differ in styling, framing and visible features, Face Comparison puts them side by side in a single report. It describes what is visible and does not identify anyone or rate who is better. Make the next photo more consistent Stand a little farther from the camera, keep the lens at eye level and use even light from the front. Relax your expression and take more than one frame. These simple changes can reduce the camera effects that are easy to mistake for facial differences. If you want to compare how lighting or angle affects the result, keep everything else the same and change just one thing between photos. Two images taken a minute apart in the same spot make a much better experiment than two photos from different years and different phones. For a related look at outline rather than balance, see our guide on finding your face shape from a photo . Why the two sides of a face differ Almost everyone has small differences between the two halves of the face. One eye may sit slightly higher, one brow may arch more, and the nose or jaw may lean a little to one side. Habits matter too: chewing on one side, sleeping on one side or smiling more strongly on one side all shape how a face looks over the years. A symmetry preview will usually find these differences, because it is built to compare the two sides. That does not mean anything is wrong. It means the tool did what it was designed to do on one frame. Mirror images can be misleading A popular trick is to mirror each half of a portrait to create two new faces. The results often look odd, and people are surprised that neither looks like them. The reason is simple: the face you recognize is the real one, with its natural differences, not a perfectly balanced version. If you try this for fun, remember that what you see depends on exactly where the centerline is placed. A small shift changes both halves, so mirror pictures are an entertaining experiment and not a measurement of anything. Keep the result in perspective The most useful outcome is often a better understanding of your photos, not a quest for perfect symmetry. If a guide shows a difference you like, such as a smile that lifts one side a little more, that is simply part of your expression. If you are curious about a change in your face and think it may be medical, a qualified professional is the right person to ask, not an app. These tools are made for adults and for entertainment and self-discovery. Scores and guides are not medical, clinical or scientific measurements. Common questions Is a facial symmetry test accurate? Not in a clinical sense. The guides on this site are illustrative and depend on the angle, lighting and expression in one photo. They are good for exploring how a portrait looks, not for measuring a face. Can my symmetry change from photo to photo? Yes. Head tilt, camera position, expression and lighting all shift the apparent balance of a face. Comparing photos taken under the same conditions is the best way to see what is the camera and what is the face. Does a more symmetrical face look more attractive? Not necessarily. Perceived attractiveness depends on many things, including expression, grooming, light and personal taste. Slight asymmetry is normal and often part of what makes a face familiar. These guides are for photo styling and creative exploration. A generated preview is not a medical assessment, a measurement guarantee, or a substitute for professional advice. /blog/seasonal-color-palette-photo-guide.body: A photo-first guide to seasonal color palettes What a seasonal palette is Seasonal color analysis sorts colors into groups named after the four seasons, usually based on how warm or cool, light or deep, and soft or clear a set of shades looks next to a person's skin, hair and eyes. The idea is that a group of colors can look harmonious on one person and less so on another. It is a popular styling framework, not a scientific law. The Seasonal Color Palette tool applies this idea to a photo. It suggests a direction and shows a set of colors as a starting point for experiments with clothes, makeup and accessories. Because it works from an image, the quality of that image matters as much as anything else. Choose a neutral starting image Color suggestions are only as dependable as the photo they start from. Daylight near a window is useful; a colored room light or beauty filter can shift the visible tone of skin, hair and eyes. If possible, compare more than one photo taken in different neutral settings. Wear a simple top and avoid very bright light bouncing from nearby walls or clothing. You are trying to see color relationships, not produce a studio portrait. Remove heavy makeup if you can, and keep your hair as it normally looks. Look for families, not rules A palette groups colors that often work together. Use it to compare muted with vivid shades, and warm-looking with cool-looking combinations. A digital preview can make those differences easier to picture, but screens and fabrics do not reproduce color identically. There is no reason to discard a favorite color because a label places it outside a season. Try the color in a different depth, fabric or position in your outfit before deciding whether it works for you. A shade that looks harsh as a collar can be lovely as a bag or a scarf worn lower down. Test colors near your face The most reliable test is physical. Hold a few fabrics or garments under your chin in daylight and look at the whole face, not just the cloth. Notice whether your skin looks brighter and more even, or whether shadows and redness stand out. Take a photo of each option so you can compare them later without relying on memory. Makeup follows the same logic. If you want to see how a lip shade from your palette reads on your own picture, the Lip Color Changer lets you compare a few shades before you buy one. Our guide to what to check in a virtual makeup try-on covers lighting and finish in more detail. Try one change at a time Start with a small experiment: a lip shade, scarf or shirt near your face. Take a photo in the same light and compare it with another option. This gives you a practical reference that is more useful than memorizing a list of permitted colors. If you would like ideas beyond color, Personalized Beauty Tips turns the visible features in your photo into a set of suggestions, and the 7-Day Glow-Up Challenge offers a gentle daily routine built from your latest scan. Both are for inspiration and self-care, not for treating any condition. Warm, cool, light, deep, soft and clear Most seasonal systems describe color along a few simple axes. Warm colors lean yellow or golden, and cool colors lean blue or pink. Light colors are pale and airy, and deep colors are rich and dark. Soft colors are muted and slightly grayed, while clear colors are bright and saturated. A person is then matched to the group whose colors share the qualities of their own coloring. If you would like to practice on your own, look at two shades of the same color, such as a warm coral and a cool pink, held against your face in daylight. The one that makes your skin look more even is the one to note. Using a palette when you shop A palette is most useful when you are choosing something new. Instead of trying to match every item you own, use it to narrow down what you try on. Take a screenshot of your suggested colors, or save the result image, and keep it on your phone for shopping trips. Remember that store lighting is often very different from daylight. If you are unsure, step near a window or outside with a garment before buying it, and check the return policy. A palette should save you time and money, not add pressure. Keep personal taste in charge A seasonal palette is a way to explore choices faster. Your preferences, culture, occasion and confidence matter just as much as a color category. If you love a shade that sits outside your suggested group, wear it. If a palette suggests something you would never choose, you can ignore that too. Results on this site are entertainment-style impressions of one photograph, and the tools are for adults aged 18 and over. Common questions Can a photo really tell me my season? A photo can suggest a direction, but it cannot replace trying colors in person. Screen settings, filters and room light all change how skin and hair appear, so treat the result as a starting point to test. What if I am between two seasons? That is very common. Many people sit between groups, and the colors that work for them come from both. Test the in-between shades near your face in daylight and keep the ones you like. Do I have to follow the palette for every outfit? No. A palette is easiest to use for pieces worn close to the face, such as tops, scarves and lip color. Trousers, shoes and bags can follow whatever you enjoy. These guides are for photo styling and creative exploration. A generated preview is not a medical assessment, a measurement guarantee, or a substitute for professional advice. /blog/natural-looking-portrait-retouch.body: How to keep a portrait retouch looking natural Decide what the photo needs A portrait may feel flat because of a dim room, an unusual color cast or a soft focus. Those are different problems from skin texture. Before applying any effect, identify the one or two distractions you actually want to address. A light adjustment to exposure or contrast can sometimes do more than a strong smoothing pass. Keep the unedited image beside the preview so it is easy to notice when the edit has gone too far. Pick the right kind of tool Different tools solve different problems. AI Skin Enhancement is aimed at evening out tone and softening the look of blemishes while keeping real skin texture visible. Smart Beauty Retouch is a one-tap portrait retouch with adjustable strength, which suits a quick all-round polish. The Face Beauty Editor lets you choose between three natural finish levels when you want finer control over smoothing and shine. If the real problem is that the photo is blurry or low resolution, smoothing will not help. The AI Face Enhancer is built for sharpening soft portraits into clearer ones. Keep in mind that it can improve clarity but cannot recover details that were never in the source image. Keep the details that make a face familiar Freckles, fine lines and natural variation in skin tone carry personality. When they all disappear, a photo can feel less like a person and more like a plastic surface. Look at the full image as well as a close crop to judge whether the face still reads naturally. Pay special attention to hair edges, glasses and the boundary between skin and background. These are places where aggressive edits can become obvious even when the center of the face looks smooth. Look at light before you look at skin Much of what people call skin problems in a photo is actually lighting. Harsh overhead light creates shadows under the eyes and highlights on the forehead and nose. Light from a flash flattens everything and exaggerates shine. Soft window light from the front or side is far kinder, and it often removes the need for heavy editing altogether. If you can retake the photo, do that first. Stand facing a window, keep the camera at eye level and wipe the lens, since a smudged lens softens detail and adds a hazy glow. A better source image gives every tool a better starting point and makes a gentle edit look more convincing. Compare before exporting Step away from the screen for a moment and reopen both versions. If the retouch is the first thing you notice, consider a gentler finish. A good edit supports the expression and lighting already in the frame. Check the result at the size it will be used. A profile picture seen at thumbnail size can take a stronger edit than a large print. If you plan to share the image widely, consider saying that it has been edited, particularly if it is for professional use. Signs that an edit has gone too far There are a few giveaways. Skin that has no pores or texture anywhere looks like a smooth surface, not like skin. Eyes that are sharper than everything around them look unnatural, and teeth that are much whiter than the rest of the image stand out. Edges that look slightly blurred or doubled around the jaw, the hair or the shoulders suggest that an effect has bled into the background. Another sign is that the person looks different from how they look in real life. A good retouch makes someone look like a well-rested version of themselves on a good day, not like a different person. A simple workflow you can repeat First, choose the best source photo you have: sharp, evenly lit and free of heavy filters. Second, make one change at a time and compare it with the original. Third, view the result at the size you will use it and at full size. Fourth, wait a few minutes, then look again with fresh eyes. If a change is only visible when you flick between before and after, it is probably subtle enough to look natural. If you can see it at once, consider reducing the strength. When to leave a photo alone Not every photo needs editing. A candid portrait with natural light, a real smile and a bit of texture often looks better untouched than a polished version. If you find yourself reaching for an edit out of habit, try posting the original and see how it feels. Editing works best as a deliberate choice for a specific reason: an important profile photo, a print for a relative, or fixing one distracting detail. Used that way, it supports the photo instead of replacing it. A note on skin health Retouching changes how skin looks in a picture; it does not change the skin. If you are interested in looking after your skin itself, general guidance from a qualified source is a better place to start than an app. The American Academy of Dermatology publishes advice on everyday sun protection , which is a good example of the basics worth knowing. The AI Skin Analysis tool describes visible features such as texture and tone variation in a photo. It cannot diagnose a condition, measure hydration or replace a clinician. If you are worried about a mark, a change in a mole or any skin symptom, ask a doctor or dermatologist. Photo-based skin tools are for visual editing and exploration, made for adults, and are not medical advice. Common questions How do I stop a retouch from looking fake? Use a light touch, keep skin texture visible and compare the result with the original at full size. If the edit is the first thing you notice, lower the strength or choose a gentler finish. Will an enhancer fix a blurry photo? It can make a soft portrait look clearer, but it cannot recover detail that was never captured. A sharper, better-lit source photo will always give a better result. Can a retouch tool improve my actual skin? No. It changes how skin looks in a picture only. For skin care, use guidance from a qualified professional or a trusted health source such as a dermatology association. These guides are for photo styling and creative exploration. /blog/plan-a-hair-change-with-a-preview.body: Plan a hair change with a photo preview | AI Beauty Styling Why preview a hair change first A haircut or a new color is one of the easiest ways to change how you look and one of the harder things to undo. Hair grows slowly, color can be expensive to correct, and a style that looks good on a model may not suit your texture or routine. A virtual preview will not remove that risk, but it can help you rule out ideas and explain the ones you like before you sit in the chair. A hairstyle changer takes your own photo and shows how a different cut or color might look around your face. That is more useful than browsing pictures of other people, because the proportions, skin tone and background are yours. Give the preview a clear starting point Use a portrait with the hairline and sides of the head visible. Strong shadows, a hat or hair covering much of the face can make it harder to understand how a new silhouette would sit around your features. A front-facing image is useful for comparing overall shape. If you are seriously considering a cut, collect a side view as well so a stylist can see your current length and texture. Natural light and a plain background help the tool separate hair from everything else. Compare shape before detail First look at the outline: where does the volume sit, and how does the length change the frame around your face? Then look at the fringe, parting or color. This order keeps you from choosing a style only because its finishing details look attractive in a mockup. The Hairstyle Changer shows four distinct cuts and styles on your photo, which is enough to compare a few directions side by side. If you are not sure which outline works with your features, the Face Shape Analyzer can give you a starting description, and our guide to finding your face shape from a photo explains how to use it sensibly. Try color separately from cut Color and cut are two separate decisions, and it helps to judge them one at a time. The AI Hair Color Changer previews five shades, from natural browns to a bold pastel, on the same photo. Looking at color on its own tells you whether you like the tone against your skin and eyes without being distracted by a new shape. Remember that real hair color depends on your starting color, previous dye and the hair's condition. A preview shows an idea of the result, not what a colorist can achieve in one visit. Ask your stylist how many sessions a big change would take. Beards and facial hair The same approach works for facial hair. AI Beard Styling previews different beard shapes and lengths on your portrait, so you can compare a short stubble with a fuller shape before you stop shaving. As with hair, texture and growth patterns vary a lot, and patchy areas may not fill in the way a preview shows. Questions to ask before you commit A preview shows how a style might look on one day, in one photo. Real life adds questions the picture cannot answer. How long does the style take to do each morning? Does it need regular trims, and how often? Will it suit the weather where you live? How will it look in a ponytail or when it grows out? Write these questions down and ask your stylist. A good stylist will be happy to talk about maintenance and will tell you honestly if a style is likely to be difficult for your hair type. Hair color and your starting point Color changes depend heavily on where you begin. Going from dark brown to a light pastel usually means lightening the hair first, which can take more than one visit and needs careful aftercare. Going from a light shade to a darker one is usually simpler, but it can be harder to reverse. Use the preview to choose a direction, such as warmer or cooler, lighter or deeper, and let a colorist suggest the way to get there safely. If you have a sensitive scalp or have had a reaction to hair dye before, say so, and ask about a patch test. Keeping the change in proportion Big changes feel exciting in a preview and can feel startling in the mirror. If you are unsure, take a smaller step first: a few inches off the length, a softer shade, or a fringe that can be grown out. You can always go further at the next appointment, but you cannot easily add length back. A friend's honest opinion is also worth asking for. Show them two or three previews and notice which one they react to, since a second view often shows you something you have missed. Bring a useful reference to the salon Save the preview alongside a photo of your current hair and one or two real-world examples. Explain which part of the idea you like, whether that is the length, the shape or the color, rather than asking for a pixel-perfect copy. Hair texture, density and growth pattern matter in real life. A generated image cannot promise that a cut will fall exactly the same way after a wash or without styling. Ask your stylist what daily care the style needs and how it will grow out. The best preview starts a conversation. It makes an unfamiliar idea easier to describe while leaving room for professional judgment and your daily routine. Common questions Will my real haircut look like the preview? Not exactly. A preview shows an idea of a style on your photo. Your hair texture, density, growth pattern and how it is cut and styled will all affect the real result, so use it as a reference for a conversation with your stylist. What photo works best for a hairstyle preview? A clear, front-facing portrait in even light with your hairline and the sides of your head visible. Avoid hats, heavy shadows and photos where hair covers much of your face. Can I preview a color without changing my cut? Yes. /blog/virtual-makeup-try-on-lighting.body: What to check in a virtual makeup try-on | AI Beauty Styling What a virtual try-on is good for A virtual makeup try-on applies a shade to a photo so you can judge it before you buy or apply anything. It is best at answering broad questions: is this family of colors flattering, would a bolder or softer version suit the occasion, and does this shade clash with what I usually wear? It is less good at telling you exactly how a particular product will look, because formulas, coverage and skin all vary. Think of it as a shortlist maker. It helps you narrow a wall of options to two or three that are worth testing in person. Start with visible features Choose a clear portrait in even light. For lipstick, keep the lips unobscured and avoid an existing strong shade. For eye looks, a forward-facing photo with open eyes makes the placement easier to understand. A filtered or underexposed image can make a shade appear brighter or duller than it would in person. Try another photo before dismissing a color that surprises you. Lips: shade and finish With the Lip Color Changer you can try shades from soft nudes through berry to a classic red, in matte or glossy finishes. Compare at least two shades on the same photo so you are judging them against each other rather than against your memory of a lipstick. Look at how the shade sits next to your teeth and skin, and how bold it feels in the full portrait. A shade that looks stunning in a close crop can feel heavy in a full-face view, and the finish changes the mood: matte looks more graphic, gloss looks softer and fresher. Eyes and brows For eye makeup, the Eyeshadow Try-On shows palettes on your own eyes, which helps you judge how colors work with your eye color and lid shape. Keep your eyes open and your gaze straight ahead in the source photo, since closed or downcast eyes hide the area where the color sits. Brows frame the whole face, and small changes make a visible difference. AI Eyebrows lets you try different shapes and thickness. Go gently: a preview that exaggerates a shape can look striking on screen yet be very different from what your natural brows can achieve. Colored contacts need extra care The Colored Contacts Try-On shows how a different eye color, such as blue, green, hazel or gray, looks on your photo. It is a cosmetic image preview only. Real lenses are different. In the United States the FDA treats decorative contact lenses as medical devices and explains that they should be fitted and prescribed by an eye-care professional, even when they do not correct vision; see its page on decorative contact lenses . If you are thinking about real lenses, talk to an optometrist or ophthalmologist rather than relying on a visual effect. Lighting changes everything Light is the single biggest reason a preview differs from reality. Warm indoor bulbs push everything toward yellow and orange, which makes a pink lipstick look more coral. Cool daylight pushes toward blue and can make a warm shade look flat. Overhead lights cast shadows around the eyes and make shadow colors look darker than they are. For the most reliable comparison, take your source photo near a window in the daytime, facing the light, with the camera at eye level. Try two photos in different light if you can, and see which shades are stable and which change a lot. Screens, skin tone and swatches Screens are another variable. Brightness, night mode and color settings change how a shade appears, so the same image can look different on two devices. Your own skin tone also affects how a color looks when it is applied, since most makeup is slightly translucent and blends with what is underneath. That is why a swatch on your hand or jawline in daylight is a good final check. Use the preview to narrow the choice, and the swatch to decide. Building a simple comparison routine A routine makes previews more trustworthy. Take one neutral photo in daylight and use it for every shade, so the only thing that changes is the color. Keep a note of the shades you try and what you thought, and give each one a quick rating from the full-face view, not just the crop. After a week, look again at your top two. If you still like both, they are the ones to buy as samples or swatch in a shop. If you have lost interest in one, you have saved yourself a purchase. Judge the whole look and use it as a shopping reference A shade can look striking in a close crop yet feel different next to your hair, clothes and skin tone. Step back to view the full portrait. Consider whether the finish, whether soft, matte, glossy or bold, fits the occasion you have in mind. Save one or two directions you like and compare them with real swatches when possible, ideally in daylight. If you also want to explore the colors that suit your hair and skin more generally, our guide to seasonal color palettes is a good companion. A try-on should make experimentation easier, not turn beauty into a set of rules. Keep the choices that feel comfortable and interesting to you. Common questions Will the real lipstick look exactly like the preview? Not exactly. The preview is a close visual idea, but formula, finish, lighting and your own lip color all change the real result. Use it to choose a direction, then test a swatch in daylight. Why does the same shade look different in two photos? Light changes how color is recorded. A warm lamp, a cool window or a phone filter can shift a shade noticeably, so compare photos taken in similar conditions. Is it safe to buy colored contacts based on a preview? A preview only shows how a color might look in a picture. Contact lenses, including decorative ones, should be fitted and prescribed by an eye-care professional. /blog/virtual-outfit-preview-limits.body: What a virtual outfit preview can tell you What an outfit preview is for Online shopping removes the fitting room, and that is the main reason people return clothes. A virtual outfit preview tries to bring part of it back: you give it a photo of yourself and an image of a garment, and it shows an image of how that garment might look on you. It is a way to explore a color, a cut or a style before you spend money. It is worth being clear about what that means. The result is a generated picture. It can say useful things about color and overall silhouette. It cannot say anything reliable about size, stretch, comfort or how a fabric moves. Use a photo that shows the garment area A clothing preview needs enough of the body in frame to place the garment. Stand naturally, keep arms from covering the outfit area when possible, and avoid a crop that cuts off the part you want to evaluate. If you are adding a garment reference, choose a clean image with the shape and details visible. A busy background or folded item makes it harder to imagine the complete look. A product photo on a plain background, or a garment laid flat, usually works best. Compare the visual direction With Virtual Try-On: Clothes you upload a photo and a garment and review a generated preview of the combination. Look at the color next to your face and the overall silhouette. A preview can help you decide whether to explore a style further or compare two ideas before shopping. It cannot prove how fabric drapes when you walk, where a seam will land, or whether a size will feel comfortable. Those details still require measurements, product information and, ideally, a real fitting. Check color against your palette Color is the part of an outfit a preview handles best. If you have already explored the shades that suit you with the Seasonal Color Palette , use the preview to see how a garment's color sits near your face. Our guide to seasonal color palettes explains how to test colors in real light so that you can confirm what you see on screen. Screens vary, so a rust orange on your laptop may look brighter or duller on your phone. Judge color in more than one place and read the product description. Other style previews Style is more than clothes. The AI Tattoo Generator previews one of three original tattoo motifs on your skin, which is a safe way to think about placement and size before making a permanent decision. Treat it as a mood-board tool: a real tattoo artist will adapt the design to your body and skin. The Silhouette Preview shows how a garment's fit shapes your silhouette. It is meant for exploring how clothes sit, not for judging your body. If a preview changes proportions in a way that does not match you, trust your original photo and the garment's real measurements. Getting a better source photo The quality of a try-on depends on the photo you start with. A straight-on image with your full torso visible and your arms relaxed at your sides gives the tool the clearest view of where a top or dress would sit. Tight, plain clothing underneath helps, because loose layers can confuse the placement of the new garment. Avoid mirror selfies with a phone covering your body, strong backlight that turns you into a silhouette, and angles taken from below or above, which distort proportions. A friend taking the photo from a short distance often gives a much better result than a selfie. Questions a preview cannot answer Even a convincing image leaves a list of practical questions. Does the fabric stretch or hold its shape? Is it see-through under bright light? Will it wrinkle in the first hour? Does the size chart match your measurements? Is the garment cut for a different height? Read reviews with photos from real customers, check the material and care label, and measure a garment you already own and like to compare it with the size chart. The preview tells you how an idea might look, and the details tell you whether it will work. Using previews responsibly and kindly Previews should make shopping calmer, not more critical. If you notice that you are judging your body against an image, close the tab and come back later. The tool is there to explore color and style, and clothes should be chosen because they feel good, not because they match an ideal. If you are previewing clothes for another person, such as a gift, only use a photo you have permission to use, and let them choose what they actually wear. Keep your decision grounded Use the generated image as a mood-board reference rather than a purchase guarantee. Save it with notes about what you liked, whether that was the neckline, color or proportion, so you can search more intentionally. Before you buy, check the size chart, the fabric content and the return policy. If the preview changes body proportions unexpectedly, rely on the original photo and the garment's real measurements. The point is to explore an outfit, not to judge your body. Tools on this site are made for adults and for entertainment and self-discovery, and a generated preview is not a guarantee of fit or appearance. Common questions Does a virtual try-on show how clothes will really fit? No. It shows an image of color, pattern and apparent drape. Size, stretch, comfort and movement need measurements, product details and, ideally, a real fitting. What kind of photo should I use? A clear photo of you standing naturally, with the area where the garment would sit visible and not covered by arms or objects. Even light and a plain background help. Can I preview a garment I have not bought yet? Yes, if you have a clear image of it, such as a product photo. The preview is a visual idea of how it could look and should be combined with the real size and material information. These guides are for photo styling and creative exploration. /blog/creative-portrait-effects-responsi.body: Make a creative portrait effect feel personal Why playful effects are worth doing well Creative portrait effects are the lightest part of AI photo editing. They turn a selfie into a cartoon, a seasonal costume or a birthday card, and most of the time they are meant to be shared with friends. A small amount of care makes the difference between a result that feels like you and one that looks like any other filtered image. Most of that care happens before you press the button: choosing the right photo, picking an effect that fits the occasion, and thinking about who will see the result. Pick a portrait with character A slight smile, a favorite jacket or a familiar background can make a stylized image feel specific to you. Choose a photo where the face is clear and there is enough room around the head for the effect to develop. Very small faces, heavy blur and strong filters leave less detail to preserve. If a result feels generic, a better starting image often helps more than adding another effect. Try a direction, then compare A comic portrait and a softer illustrated portrait tell different stories. Cartoon Yourself turns a selfie into anime, 3D or comic art, so you can compare a few directions from the same photo. Ask what remained recognizable: the expression, pose, hair or personal style. Generated effects are interpretations, not faithful records. Keep the original photo nearby, particularly if you plan to share the result as part of a memory or profile. If you want a lighter touch than a full cartoon, AI Face Filters offers trending effects in one tap. Seasonal and occasion ideas Some effects belong to a moment. The AI Halloween Mask adds spooky masks and makeup for October, and the Birthday Image Generator creates a personalized card from a photo, which makes a nicer message than a generic template. If you enjoy fantasy, the Elf Name Generator gives you an elf name and portrait, and the AI Fortune Teller offers a playful face-reading fortune. Both are for fun only. They do not predict anything and should never be taken as advice. Pranks need extra thought Some effects are made for jokes between friends. The Pregnancy Joke Filter is one of them. A joke about pregnancy can land very differently depending on who sees it, and it can be painful for people who are trying to conceive, have lost a pregnancy or are dealing with something private. Use it only on your own photo or with the clear, enthusiastic agreement of the person in it, and think before posting anywhere public. Keeping the original in the picture Creative effects are more fun when you can still see yourself in them. A cartoon of you should keep your smile, your hair shape or your glasses. If you cannot recognize yourself, try a source photo with a clearer expression, or a closer crop of the face. It also helps to change one thing at a time. If you apply a cartoon effect, a mask and a filter in sequence, little of the original survives. Pick one idea, enjoy it, and save the rest for another day. Thinking about where the result will go A result that is fine in a group chat may not be suitable for a work profile, a school page or a public post. Think about the audience first. Stylized images of real people can be reshared far beyond the original conversation, and once an image is out it is difficult to take back. For anything you plan to post publicly, check that you are comfortable with it staying online for years. If you are making something for someone else, such as a birthday card, ask them what they would like and respect their answer. Choosing the right effect for the moment It helps to start from the purpose. A cartoon avatar suits a profile picture or a fun message to friends. A seasonal mask suits a party invitation. A fortune or a fantasy name suits a game night. Matching the effect to the occasion makes the result feel intentional, and it keeps you from posting something that does not fit the place where it will appear. Try two or three options on the same photo and keep the one that makes you smile. If none of them do, try a different photo. A relaxed, natural expression usually transforms better than a stiff pose, because the effect has more of your personality to work with. Share with context and consent Use your own image or one you have permission to transform. If someone else appears in the frame, ask before posting a stylized version of them. This matters for children, too: avoid uploading photos of other people's kids without a parent's agreement. Label an altered portrait when the distinction matters, for example on a profile or in a news-like context where people might take it for a real photo. A playful result works best when the people in it understand what was changed and why. Tools on this site are made for adults aged 18 and over. If you want to share a group photo while keeping bystanders private, the Face Blur tool can obscure faces, though you should review the result carefully before posting. Common questions Which photo gives the best cartoon or filter result? A clear, well-lit portrait where the face is large in the frame and there is space around the head. Avoid heavy filters, small faces and strong blur. Do the fortune and name tools predict anything? No. They are entertainment. The fortune and fantasy name are generated for fun and have no connection to your future or personality. Can I use a friend's photo? Only with their permission. Ask before transforming or sharing someone else's image, and say clearly that the picture has been edited. These guides are for photo styling and creative exploration. /blog/restore-an-old-family-photo.body: How to prepare an old family photo for restoration Handle the original gently first The best restoration starts before any software is involved. Old prints are fragile: emulsion cracks, paper curls and fingerprints leave permanent marks. Wash and dry your hands, work on a clean flat surface and hold the photo by its edges. Do not peel a photo from an album page or remove it from a frame by force, because you may tear it. Both the US Library of Congress and the US National Archives publish plain-language advice on keeping family photographs in good condition. See the Library of Congress guide to caring for your family photographs and the National Archives guide to preserving family archives for storage and handling tips from preservation specialists. Capture as much detail as you can If you have a print, scan it flat at a useful resolution. If you are using a phone, place the photo on a level surface and shoot straight down in soft, even light. Avoid flash glare and strong reflections from a glossy finish. Do not cut away the edges too early. A border can reveal where fading, folds or missing corners begin, and that context helps you judge a restoration preview. Take a second shot with the lighting angled slightly differently if the first has glare. Keep an untouched copy Save the original scan separately before editing. A restoration may reduce scratches, contrast loss and blur, but it can also infer details that the source no longer contains. The old image remains the most faithful record of what survives. Compare the faces, clothing and background in both versions. If a feature looks invented or a person no longer resembles the original, prefer a gentler result. What restoration can and cannot do Old Photo Restoration is designed to repair scratches, fading and blur in old family photos. It works by generating a cleaner version of the image, which means that where the original is missing information, the tool makes a plausible guess. Those guesses are not verified historical facts. If a face in the photo is small or very soft, the AI Face Enhancer can sharpen portraits, but the same limits apply: clarity can improve, but details that are not in the source cannot be recovered with certainty. When a result looks like a different person, trust the original. Privacy and sharing Family photographs often show people who have not agreed to be online, including relatives who have passed away and children. Before sharing a restored image publicly, think about who appears in it and whether they, or their families, would be comfortable with it. For a photo with bystanders or strangers in the background, the Face Blur tool can hide faces you do not want to share. Review the whole image afterwards, since clothing and surroundings can still identify people. If you want to bring two relatives together in one picture, Merge Portraits can blend two portraits into one image. Label a combined picture clearly so that nobody mistakes it for a real photograph taken together. Scanning tips that make restoration easier A flatbed scanner gives the most even result. Clean the glass with a soft cloth, place the print face down and scan in color even if the photo is black and white, since color scans often capture subtle tones that help with later repair. Save the scan in a lossless format such as TIFF or PNG for your archive, and make a smaller copy for sharing. If you are using a phone, turn off the flash and take the photo in bright, even light such as by a window on an overcast day. Hold the phone parallel to the print so that the edges do not slant, and take several shots to choose from. Dealing with specific kinds of damage Different damage needs different expectations. Scratches and dust spots are usually easy to reduce. Fading and color shifts can often be improved, although the original tones are a matter of judgment. Torn or missing areas are the hardest, because the tool has to invent what was there, and the result may not match the truth. Water stains, mold and cracking emulsion are physical problems that can get worse with handling. For a valuable or very fragile photo, consider asking a professional conservator before doing anything yourself, and scan the photo first so that the information is safe. Add the story around the image When sharing a restored photo with family, note who appears in it, an approximate date if known, and where the original came from. This information is often more valuable than a perfectly polished image. Write it on the back of the print in pencil, or in the file name and description of the scan. A good restoration helps a memory become easier to see while respecting the uncertainty in damaged parts of the photograph. Store the original, the scan and the restored copy together so that the next person to look at them can see what was changed. Common questions What resolution should I scan an old photo at? A higher resolution keeps more detail for a restoration to work with. If you are using a phone, shoot straight down in even light and fill the frame, and avoid compressing the file more than necessary. Will restoration change how people in the photo look? It can. Where the original is damaged, the tool fills in plausible detail, which may differ from reality. Always compare faces with the original and prefer a gentler result when someone looks different. Should I throw the original away after restoring it? No. Keep the original print and the untouched scan. They are the only faithful record of the photo, and a future restoration may do a better job. These guides are for photo styling and creative exploration. A generated preview is not a medical assessment, a measurement guarantee, or a substitute for professional advice.
